Summarise backtest scores

Source: R/eval-backtest.R
mt_score.Rd

Summarise backtest scores

Usage

mt_score(
  backtest,
  by = "model",
  target = c("rate", "life_expectancy", "asr", "life_expectancy_gap", "asr_gap"),
  measures = NULL
)

Arguments

backtest

An mt_backtest() result (or several combined with rbind()).

by

Grouping columns, for example c("model", "horizon").

target

"rate" (log death rates per cell, default), "life_expectancy" or "asr" (when the backtest scored these quantities, see quantities in mt_backtest()), or "life_expectancy_gap" or "asr_gap" (differences between strata, see contrast in mt_backtest()).

measures

Optional further summaries (none by default):

  • "sape": the mean standardised absolute predictive error of Raftery et al. (2013), sqrt(pi / 2) |y - median| / sd with the standard deviation sd of the predictive draws. It is scaled so that its expected value is 1 when the predictive distribution is correct and normal; a mean above 1 indicates intervals that are too narrow, below 1 too wide. Raftery et al. define it for life expectancy, so it is available for target = "life_expectancy" only. Rows whose draws have no spread (sd = 0) are left out;

  • "cov90": the empirical coverage of the central 90% intervals. Raftery et al. (2013) report the coverage of the 80%, 90% and 95% intervals with their mean half-widths; with by = c("model", "horizon") they are given by horizon;

  • "halfwidth": the mean half-widths hw80, hw90, hw95 of these intervals (Raftery et al. 2013, Table 1);

  • "revision": the mean absolute revision, the absolute change of the forecast median of a cell (stratum, age group, year) between consecutive origins of the backtest, for every cell forecast from both. Stoeldraijer et al. (2013) name robustness as a purpose of a forecast: small changes in the observations when the data are updated should result in only modest changes in the forecasts. Stoeldraijer et al. (2018) measure it by the standard deviation of the changes of the forecast for one target year between successive fitting periods. The mean absolute revision over all cells forecast from consecutive origins, each of which adds a year of data with the default origins, is a package-specific summary of these changes (reference unknown). A revision belongs to the later origin and its horizon; the first origin has none. Origins further apart than one year (for example origins = c(2005, 2007)) give revisions over several years of data.

Value

A data.table with the mean CRPS, WIS and absolute error, the root mean squared error of the median (rmse), MASE (mean of absolute error over the scale, the mean absolute year-to-year change of the training data, as the mean absolute scaled error of Hyndman and Koehler 2006; rates only), empirical coverage of the 50%, 80% and 95% intervals, mean PIT, the number of scored cells and the unit of CRPS, WIS and absolute error (log rates, or years for life expectancy). Backtests of the same model with different preprocessing (column prep) are scored separately. With measures, the columns sape, cov90, hw80, hw90, hw95 and revision follow.

References

Hyndman RJ, Koehler AB (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting 22(4): 679-688.

Raftery AE, Chunn JL, Gerland P, Sevcikova H (2013). Bayesian probabilistic projections of life expectancy for all countries. Demography 50(3): 777-801. doi:10.1007/s13524-012-0193-x

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2013). Impact of different mortality forecasting methods and explicit assumptions on projected future life expectancy: the case of the Netherlands. Demographic Research 29(13): 323-354. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2013.29.13

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2018). Comparing strategies for matching mortality forecasts to the most recently observed data: exploring the trade-off between accuracy and robustness. Genus 74: 16. doi:10.1186/s41118-018-0041-y

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2012)
bt <- mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = 2007, h = 5, n_draws = 100)
mt_score(bt, by = c("model", "horizon"))
#>                     model horizon       crps        wis        mae       rmse
#>                    <char>   <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>
#> 1: Random walk with drift       1 0.04454219 0.03992641 0.06272241 0.09469268
#> 2: Random walk with drift       2 0.04654157 0.04148880 0.06166271 0.09425197
#> 3: Random walk with drift       3 0.05565911 0.04972059 0.07710375 0.11415199
#> 4: Random walk with drift       4 0.05812890 0.05190181 0.07358098 0.11643492
#> 5: Random walk with drift       5 0.06429823 0.05740455 0.08308110 0.12352441
#>        mase     cov50     cov80     cov95  pit_mean     n     unit
#>       <num>     <num>     <num>     <num>     <num> <int>   <char>
#> 1: 1.048261 0.4859155 0.7253521 0.8661972 0.5020423   142 log rate
#> 2: 1.157779 0.6126761 0.8591549 0.9718310 0.5157746   142 log rate
#> 3: 1.386932 0.6478873 0.8943662 0.9647887 0.4927465   142 log rate
#> 4: 1.287454 0.7183099 0.9577465 1.0000000 0.4763380   142 log rate
#> 5: 1.459025 0.7605634 0.9507042 1.0000000 0.4895070   142 log rate
# life expectancy: SAPE and 90% coverage by horizon (Raftery et al. 2013),
# revisions between consecutive origins
bl <- mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = 2004:2007, h = 5, n_draws = 100,
                  quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score(bl, by = c("model", "horizon"), target = "life_expectancy",
         measures = c("sape", "cov90", "revision"))
